1079.title: Six pairs
1079.hook: calm, lightness, softness, workability, skill and straightness, in body and in mind
1079.howItsDone: Abhidhamma students learn the six pairs as part of the beautiful factors, and some meditation teachers point to tranquility, lightness and pliancy of body and mind as signs that practice is settling.

segments.voice: Yesterday, sobhana, the beautiful factors: faith, mindfulness, conscience, concern, an open hand, a friendly face, balance. Your line: the beautiful.

Cold dough tears. Push a rolling pin across it straight from the fridge and it cracks at the edges, fights back, springs into its old shape. Leave the same dough on the counter for a while and it rolls out smooth, takes any shape, does what the hands ask. Nothing was added. It just softened. Today the manual finishes its list of the beautiful factors with six qualities that sound a lot like warm dough.

The six come in pairs, and every pair has the same shape: one of the body, one of the mind. Tranquility, passaddhi: calm, the settling of agitation. Lightness, lahuta: not heavy, not dragging. Softness, muduta: not rigid, not stubborn. Workability, kammannata: fit for work, ready to be used. Proficiency, pagunnata: skill, a mind that runs well. And straightness, ujukata: not crooked, without twists or tricks. A note on body. In the Abhidhamma, the body in these pairs means the cluster of mental factors, the mind's own small body, not flesh and bone. Still, some teachers point out that these qualities can be felt physically too, in shoulders that drop, a jaw that lets go. In the Anguttara Nikaya, the Buddha describes gold being refined. Iron, copper, tin, lead and silver are worked out of it, and then the gold is pliant, workable and bright, ready for whatever ornament the goldsmith has in mind. So too, he says, a mind freed of its impurities is pliant, workable and luminous. Straightness has a Dhammapada verse of its own, in Max Müller's words: "As a fletcher makes straight his arrow, a wise man makes straight his trembling and unsteady thought, which is difficult to guard, difficult to hold back." Here's the useful part. In the manual, these qualities aren't a prize at the end of a long road. They're counted in every beautiful moment, so whenever kindness or clear seeing happens, some softness and workability are already in it. On this account, a stiff, stubborn mood can't arise in the same moment as real generosity. One is cold dough. The other rolls.

segments.voice: If you'd like, go looking for stiffness, the jaw, the shoulders, the hands, the space between the eyebrows, without forcing anything to relax. Rest attention there, let the next out-breath be a little longer, and see if the place softens on its own, the way dough does on a counter. Then check the mind the same way, and if it's gripping a thought stiffly, let it be held a little more lightly.
Six pairs. Calm, lightness, softness, workability, skill and straightness, each in the body of mental factors and in the mind. Today's word.
Your line: soft and workable. Like refined gold: pliant, and ready. See you tomorrow.

1080.title: Abstinences
1080.hook: right speech, action and livelihood as moments of mind, not just rules
1080.howItsDone: Some lay Buddhists formally take the five precepts at a temple or before a monk, and Abhidhamma students learn the three abstinences of right speech, right action and right livelihood as mental factors that arise when a wrong is refrained from.

segments.voice: Yesterday, six pairs: calm, lightness, softness, workability, skill and straightness. Your line: soft and workable.

Dinner with friends, and someone brings up a person who isn't there. A remark is ready on the tongue: a joke that would land, and sting. The mouth is already open, the laugh around the table half imagined. Then it closes again, and someone passes the bread. Nothing was said. And yet the Abhidhamma says something did happen in that moment, something specific enough to have its own name.

The manual calls it virati, abstinence, and it names three. Right speech: turning away from lies, harsh words, divisive talk and idle chatter. Right action: turning away from killing, stealing and sexual misconduct. Right livelihood: turning away from earning a living in harmful ways. In the suttas these are part of the eightfold path, a way of life. In the Abhidhamma they become something smaller and sharper: a mental factor that arises in the very moment the mind turns away from a wrong it could have done. Not a rule on a wall. A moment. The commentaries tell a story to show it. A young man named Cakkana had a mother who was very sick, and a doctor said fresh hare's meat would cure her. He went to the field and caught a hare. Then, holding it, he thought: it isn't right to take one life to save another, even my mother's. He let it go. Tradition says he came home, solemnly declared that he had never knowingly harmed a living being, and his mother recovered. The commentators use the story for one kind of abstinence: refraining when the chance arrives, with no vow made beforehand. They name two more: refraining because of precepts one has taken, and a last kind that comes with awakening, when the urge is uprooted for good. The Dhammapada gathers the three doors in one verse, in Max Müller's words: "The wise who control their body, who control their tongue, the wise who control their mind, are indeed well controlled." A precept kept for years is made of moments. Each time the hand doesn't take and the tongue doesn't cut, a fresh moment of virati arises. Restraint isn't only something a person has. It's something that happens.

Not a vow, just the turning, once, here, so it's familiar when it arrives. Notice what turning away is like: a small pause, a hand that stays still, a breath.

1081.title: Compassion and wisdom
1081.hook: compassion, gladness and wisdom as factors that arise in a moment
1081.howItsDone: Abhidhamma students learn compassion and gladness as the two illimitables and wisdom as the faculty of non-delusion, and in some Buddhist communities people cultivate compassion and gladness through the practice of the four boundless states.

segments.voice: Yesterday, abstinences: right speech, action and livelihood as moments of mind, not just rules. Your line: a moment of restraint.

On a crowded bus, a stranger's grocery bag splits, and oranges roll down the aisle. Three people move at once, crouching, reaching under seats. Nobody decided, a moment earlier, to be a compassionate person. Something arose, and hands followed it. A minute later everyone is back on their phones. Today the manual finishes its list of mental factors with three that sound like virtues, and it treats them the way the bus just did: as moments.
screen: `ORANGES IN THE AISLE.` → `HANDS REACH.` → `BACK TO THE PHONES.`

segments.voice: The manual names two factors it calls illimitables, appamanna. Compassion, karuna: the mind moved by someone's suffering, wishing it would end. And gladness, mudita: joy at someone else's good fortune. It's the answer to envy, from aversion's family: the same good news, met with a lifted heart instead of a turned face. A puzzle comes up here. The Simile of the Cloth closes with four boundless states: loving-kindness, compassion, gladness and equanimity. So where are the other two? The commentators explain that the manual has already counted them. Loving-kindness is non-hate, the friendly face from the beautiful factors. Equanimity is balance. Only compassion and gladness need names of their own. Then the last factor: wisdom, panna, the faculty of non-delusion, the direct opposite of the fog in the troubled four: seeing a thing as it is. The Dhammapada ties wisdom to practice in one line, in Max Müller's words: "Without knowledge there is no meditation, without meditation there is no knowledge: he who has knowledge and meditation is near unto Nirvana." Now the turn. In ordinary speech, compassion and wisdom are traits: she's so compassionate, he's wise. The Abhidhamma doesn't forbid that; it's the conventional way of speaking this path met earlier this year. But in the ultimate way of speaking, compassion is a factor that arises in one moment, colors it, and passes. That cuts two ways. Nobody is stuck being uncompassionate, because the next moment is open. And nobody gets to rest on a reputation, because the oranges are rolling now. Wisdom works the same way: not a diploma, a moment of seeing clearly, and then another.
screen: `COMPASSION AND GLADNESS.` · `WHERE ARE THE OTHER TWO?` · `WISDOM: THE FOG LIFTS.` · then, large: `NOT A TRAIT: A MOMENT.`

Watch for the moment something leans toward them, a softening, a wish that it were easier for them; that's karuna, arising, so notice it, and notice it pass. If nothing comes, that's all right; just keep them in mind.
Compassion and wisdom. Compassion, gladness and wisdom: factors that arise in a moment, not traits a person owns. Today's word.
Your line: compassion is a moment. It isn't owned; it happens. Tomorrow the path turns from mind to matter.

1082.title: Matter
1082.hook: twenty-eight kinds of matter, beginning with the four great elements
1082.howItsDone: In Abhidhamma study, students learn the four great elements as qualities of matter, and in meditation some Theravada traditions teach attending to earth, water, fire and air in the body one by one.

segments.voice: Yesterday, compassion and wisdom: not traits a person owns, but factors that arise in a moment and pass. Your line: compassion is a moment.

Press a fingertip against the table, or your knee, or the arm of the chair. Something pushes back. It's hard, or soft. It's warm, or cool. Leave it there a moment and there's a faint press, a little give, maybe the beat of a pulse. For days this path has looked at the mind, factor by factor. Today the Abhidhamma turns to the other side of its world: the stuff that pushes back. It has one word for all of it, and it begins its list with four.
screen: `PRESS A FINGERTIP DOWN.` → `SOMETHING PUSHES BACK.` → `THE OTHER SIDE OF THE WORLD.`

segments.voice: You met these four in the body back on day two hundred fifty-four. Today they get a closer look. The word is rupa: form, or matter. In one sutta the Buddha plays on a verb that means to be afflicted. It's called rupa, he says, because it gets afflicted: by cold and heat, hunger and thirst, flies and mosquitoes, wind and sun. Matter, in this telling, is the part of you that can be bitten. The manual called the Abhidhammattha Sangaha counts twenty-eight kinds of matter, and it begins with four great elements: earth, water, fire and air. These aren't soil, rain, flame and wind. They're qualities. Earth is hardness and softness, what pushes back. Water is cohesion, what holds a thing together and lets it flow. Fire is heat, and cold too. Air is motion and support, the way air keeps a tire firm. Every bit of matter, the manual says, has all four, in different measure. A stone is mostly earth, yet it still holds together, has a temperature, presses. And a strange detail: in this system, water can't be touched. Put a hand in a stream, and touch meets softness, coolness and pressure: earth, fire and air. Cohesion is known by the mind, not the skin. The old suttas use the same four to look at the body: hair and bones as earth, blood and sweat as water, warmth as fire, breath as air. And of each one they say: this is not mine, this I am not, this is not my self.
screen: `RUPA: WHAT CAN BE BITTEN.` · `FOUR ELEMENTS ARE FOUR QUALITIES.` · `WATER CAN'T BE TOUCHED.` · then, large: `NOT MINE, NOT ME, NOT MY SELF.`

segments.voice: Feel the four, one at a time: earth in the weight of you on the seat, then water, the mind's sense of your body holding together as one shape. Then fire, warmth in your hands and coolness at the tip of the nose, and air, the breath pressing the chest out and letting it settle back. If attention drifts, begin again at earth.
Rupa. Form, matter: the part of the world that can be pressed, warmed, moved and bitten, beginning with four great elements. Today's word.
Your line: four great elements. Hardness, cohesion, heat and motion, in every bit of matter, your own hand included. Same time tomorrow.

1083.title: The body's matter
1083.hook: the senses, the body's life, its heat, its nourishment
1083.howItsDone: Abhidhamma students learn the kinds of matter found only in living bodies, such as the sense organs' sensitive matter and the life faculty, and some meditation teachers in the Theravada tradition guide students to feel warmth and other qualities in the body directly.

segments.voice: Yesterday, rupa, matter, and the four that head its list: hardness, cohesion, heat and motion. Your line: four great elements.

What's the difference between your hand and the table it's resting on? By yesterday's account, both are made of the same four great elements. Both are hard, both hold together, both have a temperature, both press. Yet one of them can feel the other, and the other can't. One gets warm from the inside, gets hungry, heals a cut. The table does none of that. So the manual keeps going past the four, into the kinds of matter that belong only to a living body.
screen: `YOUR HAND, AND THE TABLE.` → `THE SAME FOUR ELEMENTS.` → `ONE OF THEM FEELS.`

segments.voice: Start with the senses. In the Abhidhamma, the eye that sees isn't the eyeball. It's a fine, sensitive matter inside it, ready to be struck by color. The same sensitive matter sits in the ear, the nose, the tongue and the whole surface of the body: five doors where the world gets in. A table has none. Next, life. The manual names a kind of matter called the life faculty, which keeps the other living matter going, the way a caretaker keeps a garden watered. When it stops, the four great elements are still there, but the body is no longer alive. Then heat. Here temperature is one of the forces that keeps producing matter, moment after moment: warmth in a living body is part of what keeps it being made. And nourishment. Food, in this system, carries a subtle nutritive essence, and that essence keeps producing matter too. So the manual names four things that keep matter arising: past kamma, the mind, temperature and food. A table gets only one. A living body gets all four. Notice what the list never adds: a fifth thing, a soul or a self. A living body is matter held up by more conditions, not matter with someone hiding inside. In one sutta the Buddha says the world, its arising and its ending are found in this fathom-long body, with its perception and mind. The Abhidhamma takes him at his word and starts measuring.
screen: `FIVE SENSITIVE DOORS.` · `THE LIFE FACULTY KEEPS IT GOING.` · `HEAT AND FOOD KEEP MAKING MATTER.` · then, large: `NO ONE HIDING INSIDE.`

segments.voice: Bring your attention to your hands and notice their warmth, without deciding whether it's pleasant. Then let attention move to the belly, the chest, the back of the neck, and rest wherever there's warmth: the body doing its work, moment by moment, without your help. If you like, place one palm over the other and feel heat meeting heat.
The body's matter. The sense doors, the life faculty, and the heat and food that keep a living body being made. Today's word.
Your line: living matter. A hand and a table share the same four elements, and only one of them can feel. See you tomorrow.

1084.title: How fast
1084.hook: in the commentaries, many mind-moments pass while one moment of matter lasts
1084.howItsDone: Abhidhamma students learn the three phases of a mind-moment and the manual's comparison of mind-moments to moments of matter, and some meditation teachers in the Theravada tradition guide students to notice how quickly experience changes.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the body's matter: five sense doors, the life faculty, and the heat and food that keep a living body being made. Your line: living matter.

There's a short passage in the Buddha's discourses that sounds almost like a shrug. He says he can't think of anything that changes as quickly as the mind. So quickly, he adds, that it isn't easy to find a comparison for it. No number, no measurement, just a teacher admitting that the mind outruns his similes. The Abhidhamma and its commentaries didn't leave it there. They tried to measure it anyway.
screen: `NOTHING CHANGES SO QUICKLY.` → `HARD TO FIND A SIMILE.` → `THEY TRIED TO MEASURE IT.`

segments.voice: Start with the smallest unit. A moment of mind, a khana, has three phases: it arises, it stands, it dissolves. Then the next one arises. In this picture, nothing in between holds still long enough to be a self watching from the side. Each moment does its one job and is gone. Now set matter beside it. Matter also arises and passes, but more slowly: one moment of matter, the manual says, lasts as long as seventeen moments of mind. So while one moment of matter in your hand comes and goes, a whole run of mental moments has arisen, seen, felt and vanished. Now a blink. In the time it takes the eyelids to close and open, tradition says, a great many mind-moments pass. Some later teachers reach for huge numbers, and those can be held loosely. The point isn't the arithmetic. It's the direction: whatever you call this second is already a crowd of moments, each gone before you could name it. Why measure at all? Because of the Buddha's shrug. If nothing changes as quickly as the mind, nothing you're feeling right now is going to stay. A sharp word, a craving, a wave of fear: by the time you notice it, it's already becoming something else. The speed isn't meant to make you dizzy. It's meant to loosen the grip.

1085.title: Kamma in the moment
1085.hook: the "impulsion" moments where intention does its work
1085.howItsDone: In Theravada Abhidhamma study, students learn the series of mind-moments in a sense process, often through the commentaries' mango simile, and teachers point to the javana moments as the place where kamma is made.

segments.voice: Yesterday, how fast: one moment of matter lasting while seventeen moments of mind arise and pass. Your line: faster than a blink.

A man is asleep under a mango tree with his head covered. A ripe mango drops and brushes past his ear. He wakes, uncovers his head, and looks. He reaches out and picks the fruit up. He squeezes it, sniffs it, decides it's good. Then he eats it. The commentaries tell that simile, and every step in it stands for one stage of a single act of perception. The falling fruit, the turning, the looking, the testing. But only one step is the eating. Today, the eating.
screen: `ASLEEP UNDER A MANGO TREE.` → `LOOK, PICK IT UP, TEST IT.` → `THEN HE EATS.`

segments.voice: When something strikes a sense door, the Abhidhamma says, the mind runs a set series of moments. It turns toward the object. It sees, or hears. It receives, investigates and settles what the thing is. None of that is kamma yet. It's the man waking, looking, testing. Then come the moments the manual calls javana, usually translated impulsion, or running. In an ordinary sense process they usually run seven times in a row. This is the eating: where the mind doesn't only know the mango but takes it, likes it, wants it, pushes it away, or meets it with kindness. And this is where the manual locates kamma. Back on day three hundred seventy-two, you met the Buddha's plain words: intention is what I call kamma; having intended, a person acts by body, speech and mind. The Abhidhamma gives that sentence an address. Kamma isn't stored in some far-off ledger. It's made in these few running moments, wholesome or unwholesome, again and again, all day. So javana is where a life changes direction. You can't stop the mango from falling. You can't unsee it. But a pause, a breath, a moment of knowing what you're about to do, and the next run of javana can go a different way. After matter, a living body and the speed of it all, this is where the speed turns into a choice.
screen: `TURN, SEE, RECEIVE, SETTLE.` · `THEN JAVANA RUNS.` · `INTENTION IS KAMMA.` · then, large: `THE PAUSE BEFORE THE TAKING.`

segments.voice: Sit still and wait for an impulse: to scratch an itch, shift your weight, open your eyes, check the time. When it comes, don't follow it right away; name it quietly, wanting to move, and feel what happens in the pause. Then, if you choose to, move, knowing that you're moving.
Javana. Impulsion, the running moments after the mind knows its object, where intention does its work and kamma is made. Today's word.
Your line: where kamma is made. The mango falls either way; the taking is where a life turns. I'll be here tomorrow.
